hints: Start by reading carefully from Fig. 5.1 - find the time taken on the y-axis for 0.25% trypsin and then for 0.5% trypsin, and recall the formula for percentage change.
walkthrough:
Read the Two Times From the Graph**
Think of this as finding a starting value and a finishing value. From Fig. 5.1, at 0.25% trypsin the time is about $388 \text{ s}$ and at 0.5% trypsin the time is about $256 \text{ s}$. Shorter time means faster hydrolysis.

Apply Percentage Decrease**
Use $\text{percentage decrease} = \frac{\text{original - new}}{\text{original}} \times 100$. So $\frac{388-256}{388} \times 100 \approx 34\%$. Round to the nearest whole number as asked.

hints: Look at the overall shape in Fig. 5.1 - as trypsin concentration goes up, what happens to the time taken to become transparent and what does that tell you about rate?
Think about what limits the reaction when there is very little trypsin present compared to a lot of casein substrate.
Focus on the active site - what has to happen for casein to be broken down, and why would more enzyme molecules help?
Link more enzyme molecules to more frequent encounters with substrate and more complexes formed per unit time.
Remember what the clear solution actually means in terms of casein protein being hydrolysed to soluble products.
walkthrough:
Translate Time Into Rate**
A shorter time to become transparent means a faster rate. The curve falls steeply at first then more gradually, but time always decreases as trypsin concentration increases. So higher enzyme concentration gives higher rate of casein hydrolysis.

Why Low Enzyme Is Slow**
At low trypsin concentration there are few active sites available. Each active site can only handle one casein molecule at a time, and a new substrate cannot enter until products are released. So few enzyme-substrate complexes can form per second.

Why More Enzyme Is Faster**
Increasing trypsin concentration increases the number of free active sites. That greatly increases the chance of successful collisions between trypsin and casein. More collisions lead to more enzyme-substrate complexes formed per unit time.

Link to What You See**
Trypsin hydrolyses the cloudy casein protein into small soluble amino acids and peptides. When all casein is hydrolysed the milk changes from cloudy white to clear colourless. With more enzyme this complete hydrolysis is achieved in less time.

Final answer: As trypsin concentration increases, time to become transparent decreases so rate of hydrolysis increases. More enzyme provides more active sites, giving more successful collisions with casein per unit time and more enzyme-substrate complexes formed per unit time, so faster breakdown of casein to amino acids / soluble products giving transparent solution.

hints: Compare the two values at 25 degrees C in Table 5.1 - free is at 100% but immobilised is only 60%, so think about what being attached to a surface might do to contact with substrate.
walkthrough:
Spot the Difference at Low Temperature**
At $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ free trypsin shows 100% of maximum activity but immobilised shows only 60%. At this low temperature denaturation is not the issue, so something about immobilisation itself must reduce activity.

How Fixing Can Hinder**
Attaching the enzyme to a surface can distort its tertiary structure and change the shape of the active site, or physically block part of the active site. Free enzyme in solution also moves freely and collides more easily with substrate. Any one of these explains the lower activity of the immobilised form.
Final answer: Immobilisation alters tertiary structure / shape of active site or partly covers active sites, so fewer collisions / less binding with casein than for free enzyme in solution.

hints: Look at the high temperature end of Table 5.1 - what happens to free trypsin activity at 55 degrees C compared to immobilised trypsin?
Think about what high temperature normally does to bonds holding a protein in shape, and how holding the enzyme rigidly on a support might change that.
walkthrough:
Read the High Temperature Trend**
At $55^{\circ}\text{C}$ immobilised trypsin is at 95% activity but free trypsin has fallen to 20%. Free enzyme is losing activity fast between $35^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $65^{\circ}\text{C}$, a classic sign of denaturation.

How Immobilisation Protects**
High kinetic energy vibrates the molecule and breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the tertiary structure and the precise shape of the active site. Fixing the enzyme to a support restricts movement and stabilises those bonds, so the active site keeps its shape and can still bind casein at temperatures that denature the free enzyme.

Final answer: Immobilisation stabilises / protects trypsin from thermal denaturation, maintaining active site shape. It prevents breaking of hydrogen / ionic bonds holding tertiary structure, so immobilised enzyme remains active at 55 degrees C while free enzyme is denatured.
